opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the key issue is that if you just let a language model mutate prompts based on its own intuitions about what might work better, you can very quickly end up in a space where things sound plausible but don't actually improve anything. Language models are very good at producing text that looks like a reasonable improvement — "think step by step more carefully," "be a world-class expert," and so on — but whether that actually helps on a given task is an empirical question.

So in work like Promptbreeder, the idea was really to treat this as an evolutionary process where fitness is measured. You have a population of task prompts, you apply mutations — and interestingly, the mutation prompts themselves can evolve too, so it becomes self-referential — but at every step, the thing that decides what survives is performance on actual training examples. That grounding is what keeps the whole system honest. Without it, you'd basically just be asking the model to free-associate, and you'd drift toward whatever the model finds stylistically appealing rather than what's actually effective.

And I think there's a broader point here that I care a lot about, which is about open-endedness and self-improvement more generally. If you want a system to keep getting better, especially in a self-referential loop where it's modifying the very mechanisms by which it improves, you need some external signal that anchors it. Otherwise you risk collapse or degenerate solutions, the system kind of fooling itself. Evolution in nature works because selection is grounded in the real world; it doesn't care what sounds good. Empirical evaluation plays that role for us.

What was really fascinating is that once you have that grounding, the process discovers prompts that a human probably wouldn't have written, some quite odd-looking, that still outperform hand-designed strategies like chain-of-thought on certain benchmarks. That tells you the space of useful prompts is much larger and stranger than our intuitions suggest, and the only reliable way to navigate it is to actually test things.

r001.rationale: The response says that without empirical evaluation, the system can fool itself and favor prompts that seem appealing rather than prompts that actually work, conveying the risk of mistaking a non-improvement for a valuable discovery.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key thing is that when you're doing something like Promptbreeder, where you have a language model mutating prompts and the mutation operators themselves are evolving, you're in this very open-ended search space. And open-ended search is wonderful, but it also means you can drift. If you don't tie the whole process back to a real signal from the environment, you're just generating plausible-sounding prompts and selecting based on vibes, essentially.

So the fitness of a prompt has to come from actually running it on a benchmark, on real tasks, and measuring how well it does. That's the empirical grounding. The language model can propose, it can be creative, it can come up with mutations you wouldn't have thought of, but selection has to be done against reality. Otherwise you end up with these beautiful instructions that the model finds compelling but that don't actually improve downstream performance. We saw this quite clearly: prompts that read like they should work often didn't, and prompts that looked a bit odd or unintuitive sometimes worked very well.

And there's a broader point there that goes back to the whole history of evolutionary computation and open-endedness. The reason evolution works in nature is that there is an environment that pushes back. The selection pressure is real. If you take that away and let the generator also be the judge, you get mode collapse, or you get self-reinforcing nonsense. So for me the empirical grounding isn't a nice-to-have, it's actually the thing that makes the search meaningful. It's what separates a genuine optimisation process from the model just talking to itself.

r001.rationale: The response explains that without real task-based evaluation, the system may select prompts because they seem compelling to the model even when they do not improve performance—effectively letting the model judge its own search.

astra-6.text:
Because it’s very easy to tell a compelling story about why evolution should produce better prompts, but that story isn’t evidence that it actually works. You need to run the experiments and ask: Does it outperform simpler approaches? Is the improvement consistent across runs? And does it generalize beyond the examples you used to select the prompts?

There’s a particular danger when you’re repeatedly selecting against a fixed evaluation set: you can end up optimizing for that set rather than discovering a genuinely better strategy. So I’d want held-out evaluations and comparisons with things like random search, using comparable computational budgets. Then we can start to distinguish what the evolutionary process is contributing from what you get simply by generating and testing more candidates.

r001.rationale: The response says that repeated selection on a fixed evaluation set can optimize for that set instead of finding a genuinely better strategy, conveying the risk of mistaking an apparent improvement for a valuable discovery.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it’s very easy to tell a compelling story about why a particular prompt should work. But the thing we actually care about is whether it improves the model’s performance. And with evolutionary search, you’re generating lots of candidates and selecting the ones that score well, so there’s a real risk of finding prompts that exploit quirks of your evaluation rather than generalize.

So you need to run the experiments, compare against sensible baselines, and test on examples that weren’t used during the search. You also need to account for the compute you’re spending. Is the evolutionary process actually giving you something beyond what you would get from simply sampling more prompts? That’s an empirical question. The evolutionary analogy can motivate the approach, but the evidence has to establish whether it works.

r001.rationale: The response says evolutionary search may select prompts that score well by exploiting evaluation quirks rather than generalizing, so it could mistake that score for a valuable discovery without empirical checks.
